video_title: NextEra Energy CEO: Powering AI and Nuclear's Comeback | Podcast | In Good Company
gist: NextEra CEO John Ketchum tells NBIM's Nicolai Tangen that US power demand is now projected to rise sixfold by the mid-2040s, driven by AI data centers plus reshoring, LNG and electrification, and that NextEra's scale (about $60bn/yr capex 2027-32, supply bought through 2030) and pending Dominion acquisition position it to capture the buildout. He covers the pivot back to gas for baseload, hyperscalers bringing their own generation under ratepayer pledges, the Duane Arnold nuclear restart for Google, and why SMRs need federal last-dollar risk support and won't scale before the mid-2030s.

insights.claim: NextEra CEO John Ketchum says US power demand, static for years, is now expected to increase sixfold over the next 20 years, reaching that projection by the mid-2040s.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Utilities and power developers shift from low-growth bond proxies to growth capex stories.
insights.quote: it's expected to increase sixfold over the next 20 years

insights.claim: Ketchum says the demand inflection materialized only about 24 months ago, driven by the pace of AI adoption and capex from hyperscalers and data center operators; two to three years ago NextEra still anticipated stagnant demand.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: The speed of the forecast revision explains supply-chain tightness and repricing of power assets.

insights.claim: Ketchum stresses demand growth is broad-based, not just data centers: reshoring of manufacturing via trade policy, LNG terminals, semiconductor fabs, transportation electrification and rising residential use all add load.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Power demand thesis is less dependent on AI alone than often assumed.

insights.claim: Ketchum says only a global recession that cut AI spending and investment would make NextEra's demand outlook wrong five years from now.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Management sees AI-capex collapse as the main downside risk to the power demand thesis.

insights.claim: Ketchum argues the US cannot afford to lose the AI race to China or India because falling behind technologically would cost economic leadership and jobs, and says Europe must keep up or its economy will fall behind.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Positions AI power buildout as national-security priority, supporting policy tailwinds.

insights.claim: Ketchum says NextEra has built more generation over the last 20 years than its next 20 largest US peers combined and claims it builds, buys, operates and finances cheaper than peers due to scale.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Scale advantage is NextEra's core moat in a capex-heavy cycle.
insights.quote: we built more than the next 20 combined

insights.claim: NextEra plans to spend about $60bn a year on power plants between 2027 and 2032 — roughly a billion dollars a week — framed as a 50-state capital investment plan.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
insights.so_what: Massive capex implies large rate base and backlog growth, plus equipment demand for suppliers.

insights.claim: Ketchum says Florida Power & Light's customer bill has fallen 20% in real terms over 20 years, is 37% below the national average, and its reliability is top decile, 60% better than national average.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Affordability track record is NextEra's key argument to regulators for the Dominion deal.

insights.claim: NextEra agreed to acquire Dominion Energy, described as the biggest merger in the industry's history, to bring scale benefits to Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina.
insights.speaker: Nicolai Tangen
insights.so_what: Creates the world's largest power company; regulatory approval in Virginia is the key gating item.

insights.claim: To win Virginia approval, NextEra revised commitments to bring 1,000 new jobs to Virginia (600 from NextEra, 400 from supplier letters of intent) and build an office tower as a dual headquarters.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Signals regulatory negotiation concessions; watch for further commitments.

insights.claim: Ketchum says scale turns equipment shortages (turbines, transformers, solar panels, inverters, batteries) into a competitive advantage, since NextEra is often its suppliers' largest customer and is already buying supply through 2030.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Smaller developers face equipment access disadvantages; supply chain locked through 2030.

insights.claim: Ketchum says NextEra can build wind in 12 months, solar in 18 and battery storage in 15, versus three to four years for gas, letting it meet 'speed to power' demand on the front end.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Renewables + storage remain the fastest capacity to deploy despite the gas pivot.

insights.claim: NextEra bought a couple of data centers to learn the business but decided against owning them, instead selling co-located land to hyperscalers and supplying generation, because hyperscalers want to own and control their own data centers for security and chip refresh.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Utilities likely won't vertically integrate into data centers; land+power bundles are the play.

insights.claim: NextEra runs an annual employee-driven efficiency program (this year called 'Rewire') focused on applying AI to business processes, yielding substantial capital and O&M savings folded into its financial plan.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: AI is a cost lever for utilities; Ketchum says it has created more work, not layoffs.

themes.theme: Gas, baseload and the renewables pivot

insights.claim: Ketchum says data centers need round-the-clock baseload that 4-hour (possibly 8-hour stacked with solar) storage cannot yet provide, so NextEra has pivoted back to gas-fired generation, where it has the largest US gas fleet experience.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Gas turbine demand and gas-fired build are structural beneficiaries of AI load.

insights.claim: Ketchum says gas generation is roughly two to three times more expensive than building solar.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Baseload reliability carries a cost premium that will pressure affordability.

themes.theme: Hyperscaler contracting and data center backlash

insights.claim: Ketchum says hyperscalers increasingly contract directly with generators because excess grid supply is gone and they've signed a ratepayer protection pledge to bring their own generation rather than raise retail prices.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Bring-your-own-generation becomes the norm, favoring developers with full value-chain capabilities.

insights.claim: Ketchum says regulators including FERC (reviewing PJM, MISO, SPP) are converging on requiring data centers to pay for their own power, and Florida has codified one of the most protective large-load tariffs into statute.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Large-load tariffs shift cost risk onto hyperscalers, protecting utility affordability narratives.

insights.claim: Ketchum attributes data center backlash to community relations and job-loss fears from AI, and says responsible hyperscalers are responding with closed-loop cooling, treated wastewater, property taxes, noise/setback compliance and community investments like Meta's in Louisiana.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Social license is a growing gating factor for data center siting.

insights.claim: Ketchum says the US is very short of technical workers, and retraining the workforce is needed alongside the AI buildout.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Skilled-labor scarcity is a buildout constraint.

insights.claim: NextEra is restarting the shut Duane Arnold nuclear plant — a 'super outage' of refurbishment and refueling since the facility was left in good shape — with Google agreeing to buy its power for 25 years.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Nuclear restarts are a fast, de-risked source of firm carbon-free power for hyperscalers.

insights.claim: Ketchum says 96+ OEMs claim to make small modular reactors, and NextEra has narrowed these to three or four it views as possibly viable, favoring Gen 3 over Gen 4 due to Gen 4's added fuel risk.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Most SMR vendors are unlikely to succeed; consolidation ahead.

insights.claim: Ketchum says the key SMR question is who takes the 'last dollar' cost-overrun risk: NextEra will cap its own exposure and not burden customers, so hyperscalers, EPC contractors, undercapitalized OEMs and the federal government must share it.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: SMR deployment hinges on federal backstops; developers won't underwrite first-of-a-kind risk.

insights.claim: Ketchum expects SMRs to reach nth-of-a-kind only by the middle of the next decade or later, requiring federal support, which he says the current administration has been very supportive of.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: SMR revenue is a 2035+ story; near-term nuclear upside is restarts and existing fleets.

insights.claim: Ketchum cites NextEra's 2012 Spain solar investment, made when S&P ranked Spain among the 7-8 least risky countries (above the US at 18th), as a failure after recession-driven feed-in tariff cuts, leading to its stance of never investing more in Europe.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Regulatory/retroactive tariff risk keeps major US developers out of European renewables.

insights.claim: Ketchum describes NextEra's 'toe in the water' approach: small bets in new industries to establish positions, without overcommitting, so it can pull back quickly if hurt.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Explains measured approach to SMRs and data center ownership.

insights.claim: Ketchum says NextEra does a 10-year forecast, unusual in the industry, because long-lived capital bets made today often don't come online until year five.
insights.speaker: John Ketchum
insights.so_what: Long-horizon planning underpins supply-chain and capex advantages.
